t: For necessary expenses, not otherwise provided for, to carry out civil defense and emergency preparedness activities, including activities authorized by section 103 of the National Security Act (50 U.S.C. 404), the Strategic and Critical Materials Stock Piling Act (50 U.S.C. 98–98h–8), the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950, as amended (50 U.S.C. App. 2251–2297), and the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended (50 U.S.C. App. 2061–2166), $129,621,000 of which not to exceed $37,100,000 shall be available for allocation under section 205 of the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950, as amended.

fable.w: This is an appropriations provision that funds civil defense and emergency preparedness activities under several named statutes. The tempting reading is that the allocation under section 205 of the Federal Civil Defense Act (which involves funds to states) implies coordination with states, but the text only makes money available. It sets up no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government.
fable.s: For necessary expenses, not otherwise provided for, to carry out civil defense and emergency preparedness activities

qwen_block.w: This section is an appropriations provision that authorizes funding for civil defense and emergency preparedness activities. It does not establish any mechanism for consultation, coordination, or participation with entities outside the federal government. The reference to 'allocation under section 205' describes how funds may be distributed internally or to states, but this specific text does not mandate public participation or outside consultation.
qwen_block.s: For necessary expenses, not otherwise provided for, to carry out civil defense and emergency preparedness activities... $129,621,000 of which not to exceed $37,100,000 shall be available for allocation under section 205 of the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950, as amended.

opus.w: This section only appropriates money for civil defense and emergency preparedness. It sets aside part of the funds for allocation under section 205 of the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950. One could argue that sending money to states counts as outside involvement. It does not: grants and benefit allocations are excluded under the definition. The section also does not call for any comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, or right to sue.
opus.s: $129,621,000 of which not to exceed $37,100,000 shall be available for allocation under section 205 of the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950, as amended.

qwen_chat.w: This section is an appropriations clause that authorizes funding for civil defense activities. It mentions that funds are available for allocation under another statute, but it does not itself require or recommend any participation by non-federal entities (such as public comment, consultation with states, or advisory boards). The actors involved are the federal government (appropriating funds) and the reference to a statutory allocation mechanism, which is internal to the government's execution of its duties. There is no mention of outside parties being consulted or involved in the decision-making process described in this text.
qwen_chat.s: For necessary expenses, not otherwise provided for, to carry out civil defense and emergency preparedness activities... $129,621,000 of which not to exceed $37,100,000 shall be available for allocation under section 205 of the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950, as amended.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "allocation" implies a decision-making process involving outside parties (like states or local governments) who receive the funds. However, the text itself only authorizes the appropriation and sets a limit for allocation under another statute; it does not describe the allocation process or require any consultation, comment period, or participation by non-federal entities in this specific section. The definition requires the section itself to involve participation. This section is purely an appropriations clause.
